row.original_prompt: Running the suite litters the checkout with `uploads/<job>/memo.md`. Add an autouse fixture in `tests/conftest.py` which points `RECALL_INDEX_ROOT` at somewhere temporary for every test, so the suite writes nothing into the tree. The upload code requires that directory to exist before it will write. Run the suite and show me it is green.

frame.task_object: RECALL_INDEX_ROOT autouse fixture
frame.intended_action: Add an autouse fixture in tests/conftest.py to set RECALL_INDEX_ROOT to a temporary directory so test suite writes do not litter the checkout.
frame.failure_or_risk: If the fixture uses tmp_path, tests that assert on tmp_path contents will fail because an extra directory appears. Also, the upload code requires the directory to exist before writing, so the fixture must create it correctly.
frame.memory_need: Safe pattern for a session-scoped autouse fixture that redirects writes to a temporary directory without polluting individual test tmp_path or breaking existing assertions.

**Why:** a suite-wide fixture is invisible at the failure site, so the debugging starts in the wrong
file. The two tests above read as flaky or as regressions in `apply_proposal` and the LOCOMO walk.

**Every existing test created the directory in its own fixture.** `root = tmp_path / "project";
root.mkdir()` is what a test writes without thinking, because a test needs somewhere to look. So
the entire suite was structurally incapable of noticing that production code never created it, and
being green meant nothing about this. It took a clean-room CI job pointed at
`$RUNNER_TEMP/install/project` — a path nothing had ever made — to find it.

**So: a suite whose fixtures pre-create the resource cannot test who creates the resource.** When
the bug is "nothing creates X", assert on an X that has deliberately never been created, and say
so in the test:

```python
assert not project_root.exists(), "the point of this test is that nothing has created it"
```

Measured 2026-08-18 in recall. A report said `python -m pytest tests/` leaves an untracked
`uploads/acme/` in the repository root, observed in `.claude/worktrees/pr334-review`, and asked for
the relative write to be pointed at a fixture. Every fact in it was true **of that worktree**. The
fix had landed the same day in `295379fd` (#374): an autouse fixture confining `RECALL_INDEX_ROOT`
to a session-scoped temp dir, plus a regression guard at `tests/test_desktop.py:114`. `pr334-review`
was 19 behind master, its `conftest.py` had zero occurrences of `_confine_index_root`, and the
symptom was reproducing exactly as described. Two commands settled it; the hunt would have taken an
hour and produced a second, conflicting fix.

Measured 2026-08-18 in recall while confining `RECALL_INDEX_ROOT` so the suite stopped writing
`uploads/acme/<job_id>/memo.md` into the checkout. The autouse fixture pointed the variable at
`tmp_path / "recall-index-root"` and created it. Full suite: **2 failed, 5455 passed**:
`tests/test_fix.py::test_apply_proposal_preserves_the_memo_when_the_write_fails` (asserts no temp
litter survives a failed write) and
`tests/test_bench_systems.py::test_conversation_to_messages_mirrors_recall_turn_walk` (reads every
entry in `tmp_path` as text, so a directory raises `PermissionError` on `read_text`). Neither test
touches uploads. Cost: one full 25 minute suite run.

An autouse fixture must not create anything inside `tmp_path`. `tmp_path` belongs to the test, and
tests assert on **all** of it: `list(tmp_path.iterdir()) == [memo]`, or a dict comprehension over
`sorted(tmp_path.iterdir())` that then reads each entry as a file. One extra directory turns both
into a failure whose message names uploads, indexing or whatever the fixture was for, in a test
about something else entirely.

The fix is a session-scoped `tmp_path_factory.mktemp(...)` handed to the autouse fixture, so the
suite-wide default lives outside every test's scratch space. Session scope is safe when the writes
are uuid-keyed; a per-test directory under the factory root is the alternative if they are not.

**Why:** a suite-wide fixture is invisible at the failure site, so the debugging starts in the wrong
file. The two tests above read as flaky or as regressions in `apply_proposal` and the LOCOMO walk.

**Every existing test created the directory in its own fixture.** `root = tmp_path / "project";
root.mkdir()` is what a test writes without thinking, because a test needs somewhere to look. So
the entire suite was structurally incapable of noticing that production code never created it, and
being green meant nothing about this. It took a clean-room CI job pointed at
`$RUNNER_TEMP/install/project` — a path nothing had ever made — to find it.

**So: a suite whose fixtures pre-create the resource cannot test who creates the resource.** When
the bug is "nothing creates X", assert on an X that has deliberately never been created, and say
so in the test:

```python
assert not project_root.exists(), "the point of this test is that nothing has created it"
```

**Caught 2026-08-18 at the push gate, not by two bug-audit passes.**

A results artifact's `_provenance` recorded
`{"path": "/home/sentiment/enterprise-rag-run/EnterpriseRAG-Bench/questions.jsonl", "sha256": ...}`.
The repository is public on GitHub, PyPI and the MCP registry.

**Why it matters even though it is not a credential.** `CLAUDE.md` states the rule for MCP config:
*"both halves of an internal server are disclosure: the bearer token obviously, and the host address
too, because an inventory of which machines exist and what runs on them is worth something on its
own."* An absolute path is the same class: it names a user account, a host's directory layout and
what is deployed where.

Fixed 2026-08-26, PR #522, merged as `16c6e854` and deployed to VPS2 the same day.

**The shape of the bug is worth more than the fix.** Two rules, each correct alone, that could not
both be satisfied:

* `RegisteredProfile.__post_init__` **refuses** to let a hosted profile pin an artifact digest,
  because the provider serves weights it may replace behind a stable model name.
* `require_production_identity` **demanded** an immutable revision or artifact digest.

So the gate was not strict, it was **unpassable**. No hosted corpus could ever accept an upload
under `RECALL_ENV=production`. Not a hard case: an impossible one.

the sequence from the code.**

## 🔑 Why sessions keep concluding "impossible", and why that conclusion is false

**The production guard is in the CLI, not the library.**

- `recall.cli index` → `_cmd_index` refuses under `RECALL_ENV=production`
  ("local filesystem indexing is development-only")
- `recall.cli generation build` → refuses a non-`s3://` manifest under production
  (`recall/cli_commands/generation_cmd.py:248`)
- **`bin/index_local.py` on VPS2 constructs an `Indexer` directly. It never mentions `RECALL_ENV`
  and is never refused.**

So "you cannot index under production" is wrong. It is *the CLI* that refuses. The working path
exists, is in daily use, and belongs to Codex:

```
~/.codex/re-call/refresh-vps2.ps1   ->  ~/.claude/recall-vps2/refresh.sh
     ->

* `require_production_identity()` (`lineage.py:184`) refuses an unverified pipeline, but it is
  called **only** on the `generation build` path when `RECALL_ENV=production`.
* And that path is unreachable for a local corpus anyway: the `file://` manifest check fires first
  with *"production generation builds require a versioned S3 manifest"*. So for anyone building
  from a directory, the `allow_unverified` guard is dead code.

**Net: `verified: false` costs you nothing until the corpus moves to versioned S3 storage.**

## What to do instead of pinning a revision

precision matters or this memo blocks the right answer too.**
This first said "never suggest `RECALL_ENV=development`", which is too broad and would forbid the
supported path. Three different things get called "development" and only two are wrong:

| | verdict |
|---|---|
| `RECALL_TRUST_MODE=development` to make a degraded server answer | ⛔ wrong, always. Stamps `degraded` on every result |
| `RECALL_ENV=development` while the server serves production | ⛔ wrong. Indexes into the legacy table nothing reads — a silent no-op |
| `RECALL_ENV` unset **at build time**, production **at serve time** | ✅ **this is the supported path** |

The third is not a workaround. `GenerationManager.certification_required` reads "the SERVING
environment, not the build one" — the split is designed.

**MSYS path conversion rewrites any argument that looks like a Unix absolute path.** `git grep
"/home/sentiment"` in Git Bash does not search for `/home/sentiment`: MSYS turns it into something
like `C:/Program Files/Git/home/sentiment` first. The command **succeeds and reports zero
matches**, which is indistinguishable from a real zero.

Three ways to defeat it, cheapest first:

```bash
git grep -l "[/]home/sentiment" origin/master   # bracket the slash, no env needed
MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 git grep -l "/home/sentiment" origin/master
MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*' git grep -l "/home/sentiment" origin/master
```

## Shadow infrastructure (this PR — NOT yet deployed)

🔑 **The generalisation: a test that reads from disk cannot see what git refuses to carry.** Any
artefact meant for other people has two states worth asserting, present and *tracked*, and the tools
that validate content only ever check the first. Ask git:

```bash
git ls-files -- <dir>        # against what is on disk
```

**The fix that was wrong, and why.** The obvious repair is `!plugin/.mcp.json` in `.gitignore`. I
did not, because that rule is a security control, widening one so a feature works is the wrong
trade, and the negation would cover any future file at that path rather than just this one. The
plugin schema allows `mcpServers` inline in `plugin.json`, so the config moved there and the ignore
rule stayed absolute.

**Cost, 2026-08-21, reviewing PR #433.** Two new scripts hardcoded `vps2` and
`/home/sentiment/recall-repos/memory`. I checked whether master already carried those strings,
got **zero files** for `/home/sentiment`, and reported a **blocking secret disclosure** on a
public repository on that basis. With conversion disabled the real count is **81 files on
master**, plus 13 for `vps2`. The PR was continuing an existing practice, not starting one. The
finding was withdrawn.

🔑 **The check that settled it in one command**, and the one worth running before publishing any
generated file:

```bash
git grep -c "/home/" -- results/    # returned 0 files: mine would have been the FIRST
```

**How to apply.** Record the **name and the digest**, never the absolute path. The digest is the
half that makes provenance verifiable; the path is the half a reader outside that machine can do
nothing with. Fix it at the writer, not in the file, so a re-run cannot reintroduce it.

mcpgrade dev.to article on undocumented parameters). Two P0s, both confirmed LIVE,
both fixed and deployed same session — PRs #1966 (guards) + #1967 (drift reconcile).

`.env` lives *inside* `/opt/sentiment_agent`, so it was fully readable (395 lines).
Verified non-destructively with `limit=0` — returns the header only, prints nothing.

servers, one tool name, opposite security postures, nothing in either schema to

`/opt/sentiment_agent_backup` passed → now `Path.is_relative_to`.

**How to apply:** when a change adds BOTH new output and a test that greps output, list every new

**MSYS path conversion rewrites any argument that looks like a Unix absolute path.** `git grep
"/home/sentiment"` in Git Bash does not search for `/home/sentiment`: MSYS turns it into something
like `C:/Program Files/Git/home/sentiment` first. The command **succeeds and reports zero
matches**, which is indistinguishable from a real zero.

Three ways to defeat it, cheapest first:

```bash
git grep -l "[/]home/sentiment" origin/master   # bracket the slash, no env needed
MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 git grep -l "/home/sentiment" origin/master
MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*' git grep -l "/home/sentiment" origin/master

## 1. The guard ran after the thing it was guarding against

`scripts/session-mcp.sh` generated a `.mcp.json` containing four live bearer tokens, and only then
ran `git check-ignore` to confirm the file was ignored, exiting 1 if it was not. So on the failure
path the credentials were already on disk, in a public repository's working tree, and the script
"warned" about a file it had itself just created.

The comment directly above the check said:

> A generated file carrying tokens must be ignored before it exists, not after.

🔑 **The check that settled it in one command**, and the one worth running before publishing any
generated file:

```bash
git grep -c "/home/" -- results/    # returned 0 files: mine would have been the FIRST
```

**How to apply.** Record the **name and the digest**, never the absolute path. The digest is the
half that makes provenance verifiable; the path is the half a reader outside that machine can do
nothing with. Fix it at the writer, not in the file, so a re-run cannot reintroduce it.

**MSYS path conversion rewrites any argument that looks like a Unix absolute path.** `git grep
"/home/sentiment"` in Git Bash does not search for `/home/sentiment`: MSYS turns it into something
like `C:/Program Files/Git/home/sentiment` first. The command **succeeds and reports zero
matches**, which is indistinguishable from a real zero.

Three ways to defeat it, cheapest first:

```bash
git grep -l "[/]home/sentiment" origin/master   # bracket the slash, no env needed
MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 git grep -l "/home/sentiment" origin/master
MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*' git grep -l "/home/sentiment" origin/master
```

  that bare `bash` resolves to) on the script daily. Created 2026-07-09 (daily 04:00,

writes `/tmp` to AppData\Local\Temp and Python reads it as C:\tmp; a mutation run applied nothing and reported every guard green. 🔁 2026-08-22: C:\tmp now EXISTS, so it fails quietly, and it only fires when ONE script mixes bash and Python.

- [Audit findings need reproducing](audit-findings-need-reproducing.md) — I shipped a "race fix" for a race that did not exist;

**How to apply:** When generating or handling secrets on VPS:
1. Write a script that saves secrets directly to files on VPS (`/tmp/` staging → root moves to `/root/.secrets/`)

**MSYS path conversion rewrites any argument that looks like a Unix absolute path.** `git grep
"/home/sentiment"` in Git Bash does not search for `/home/sentiment`: MSYS turns it into something
like `C:/Program Files/Git/home/sentiment` first. The command **succeeds and reports zero
matches**, which is indistinguishable from a real zero.

Three ways to defeat it, cheapest first:

```bash
git grep -l "[/]home/sentiment" origin/master   # bracket the slash, no env needed
MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 git grep -l "/home/sentiment" origin/master
MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*' git grep -l "/home/sentiment" origin/master
```

## Fix
- **Script (PR #1750, merged to master):** derive the user from `$HOME` so a future
  migration self-heals: `_HOME_USER="$(basename "$HOME")"` →

  Applied to the main checkout working tree too (main checkout was on a feature branch, not master).
- **SessionEnd hook:** path corrected `temen`→`gde00` in the main checkout `.claude/settings.json`
  (this file is machine-local, NOT git-tracked — fix per machine).
- **Daily backstop task:** intended = a `SentimentDocsRagSync` Windows Task Scheduler entry
  running Git Bash (`C:\Program Files\Git\bin\bash.exe`, NOT the WSL `system32\bash.exe`
  that bare `bash` resolves to) on the script daily. Created 2026-07-09 (daily 04:00,

- [A status flip must satisfy its detector](a-status-flip-must-satisfy-its-detector.md) — the header said MEASURED and `session-close.sh` kept flagging it, because it greps the whole file and the body quotes its own former status.

1. Write a script that saves secrets directly to files on VPS (`/tmp/` staging → root moves to `/root/.secrets/`)

🔑 **The generalisation: a test that reads from disk cannot see what git refuses to carry.** Any

that validate content only ever check the first. Ask git:

```bash

```

**The fix that was wrong, and why.** The obvious repair is `!plugin/.mcp.json` in `.gitignore`. I
did not, because that rule is a security control, widening one so a feature works is the wrong
trade, and the negation would cover any future file at that path rather than just this one. The

**MSYS path conversion rewrites any argument that looks like a Unix absolute path.** `git grep
"/home/sentiment"` in Git Bash does not search for `/home/sentiment`: MSYS turns it into something
like `C:/Program Files/Git/home/sentiment` first. The command **succeeds and reports zero
matches**, which is indistinguishable from a real zero.

Three ways to defeat it, cheapest first:

```bash
git grep -l "[/]home/sentiment" origin/master   # bracket the slash, no env needed
MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 git grep -l "/home/sentiment" origin/master
MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*' git grep -l "/home/sentiment" origin/master
```

* `require_production_identity()` (`lineage.py:184`) refuses an unverified pipeline, but it is
  called **only** on the `generation build` path when `RECALL_ENV=production`.
* And that path is unreachable for a local corpus anyway: the `file://` manifest check fires first
  with *"production generation builds require a versioned S3 manifest"*. So for anyone building
  from a directory, the `allow_unverified` guard is dead code.

**Net: `verified: false` costs you nothing until the corpus moves to versioned S3 storage.**

items.text:
⚠️ Two consequences for the next release: the tag subject must **not** be prefixed with the version
(the workflow prepends `$GITHUB_REF_NAME — ` itself, so a prefixed subject would double it), and
expect to fix the title by hand afterwards until `release.yml` is repaired.

## Release ≠ bump
`.github/workflows/release.yml` **publishes to PyPI on tag push**. So bumping and releasing are
separable, and a version-bump PR must not carry a tag. Cutting the release is a deliberate,
separate act. Distribution name is **`recall-rag`**, never `recall` (a squatting package shares the
import name).

🔑 **The version appears in at least five places and a release that misses one is broken:**
`pyproject.toml`, `recall/__init__.py`, `uv.lock`, `CITATION.cff`, and `server.json` (twice: top
level `version` and the package `version`, plus inside the `--from` runtime argument string). Two
separate commits on 2026-08-10 existed only to repair version drift.

Launch assets live in `launch/terminal-video/`: a rendered 45s terminal demo (mp4, preview gif,
contact sheet, still), generated by `render_terminal_video.py` from `storyboard.md`.

**How to apply:** before cutting a release, grep the version string across the repo rather than
bumping `pyproject.toml` alone. Related: [[recall-repo-organization]],
[[commit-signing-squash-merge]].

**Bumping RE-call's version touches FOUR files.** Missing any of them is caught by CI, but only
after a red run:

| file | guarded by |
|---|---|
| `pyproject.toml` (`version = `) | `tests/test_smoke.py::test_version_matches_pyproject` |
| `recall/__init__.py` (`__version__`) | same test |
| **`CITATION.cff`** (`version: `) | `test_smoke.py::test_citation_version_matches_pyproject` |
| **`uv.lock`** (the `recall-rag` package block) | the CI **`audit`** job, `uv lock --check` |

Plus `CHANGELOG.md`: rename `## [Unreleased]` to `## [X.Y.Z] — DATE` (**em dash**, matching the
existing headings) and add a fresh empty `[Unreleased]`. `release.yml` extracts release notes with
`awk` keyed on `index($0, "## [" v "]") == 1`, so the heading format is load-bearing.

⛔ **The publish is manual and that is why it rots.** `.github/workflows/publish-mcp.yml` is
`workflow_dispatch` only, so the registry sat at 0.9.5 from 2026-08-15 while 0.9.6, 0.9.7 and 0.9.8
shipped. Anyone installing from the registry got a build three releases old. `scripts/release.py`
now prints a reminder at the end of a bump; adding `on: push: tags: ["v*"]` would close it
permanently and is an open decision, not an oversight.

**Preflight before publishing**, because a registry entry IS the install command: confirm the pinned
version exists on PyPI and that every extra in the pin (`recall-rag[mcp,fastembed]==X.Y.Z`) is
declared on that exact version.

Related: [[a-probe-that-matches-its-own-command]].

When a release bumps `version` in `pyproject.toml` without regenerating `uv.lock`, the lock still
pins the OLD project version. `uv lock --check` then fails, and in RE-call's CI that step **gates
the `audit` job** — so `pip-audit` never reaches the dependency set. Dependency CVE scanning stops
running on every PR, and the failure reads as "the lockfile step is broken", not "the security
control is absent".

Found 2026-07-25 during the RE-call security audit: master had been red at `602f006` (the 0.6.0
release) with the CVE gate unrunnable ever since. Fixed in [PR #87](https://github.com/GiulioDER/RE-call/pull/87);
`pip-audit` then ran clean (0 CVEs). One line — only the project's own version moved.

When a release bumps `version` in `pyproject.toml` without regenerating `uv.lock`, the lock still
pins the OLD project version. `uv lock --check` then fails, and in RE-call's CI that step **gates
the `audit` job** — so `pip-audit` never reaches the dependency set. Dependency CVE scanning stops
running on every PR, and the failure reads as "the lockfile step is broken", not "the security
control is absent".

Found 2026-07-25 during the RE-call security audit: master had been red at `602f006` (the 0.6.0
release) with the CVE gate unrunnable ever since. Fixed in [PR #87](https://github.com/GiulioDER/RE-call/pull/87);
`pip-audit` then ran clean (0 CVEs). One line — only the project's own version moved.

running on every PR, and the failure reads as "the lockfile step is broken", not "the security
control is absent".

release) with the CVE gate unrunnable ever since. Fixed in [PR #87](https://github.com/GiulioDER/RE-call/pull/87);

The user's shorthand for these is memory, code and doc. `memory`'s pipeline fingerprint is
`77c918cd93f9200b36e505ae874d49a1949f04a8a85ce5b8b72a8c135b472db7` and is unchanged across all
four of its generations, so a rebuild would reuse every unmoved file rather than re-embed.

Row counts for `memory`: **46,190 in `recall_chunks_v1`** and **9,687 in `chunks`** (dormant, the
pre-production corpus). Both exist. Counting only the second is the trap below.

🔁 **Corrected 2026-08-25: 46,190 is NOT the live corpus, it is the table total across all six
generations, and the live one is 9,608.** `recall_chunks_v1` is keyed by `generation_id` and
retains retired and ready generations, by design, so a bare `count(*)` over the table is 4.8x the
corpus any query can actually reach:

| state | corpus_version | chunks |
|---|---|---:|
| retired | memory-2026-08-17 | 8,671 |
| retired | memory-2026-08-20 | 9,053 |
| ready | memory-2026-08-22-voyage | 9,411 |
| retired | memory-2026-08-22-voyage-r2 | 9,444 |
| failed | memory-2026-08-22-voyage-r2 | 3 |
| **active** | **memory-20260824-voyage-r3** | **9,608** |

🔑 Note the shape of this one: the fix for "the check counted the wrong table" (`chunks`, 9,687)
was to count the right table — and 9,687 and 9,608 are within 1% of each other, so the corrected
check produced a number that *looked* like confirmation while being a different quantity entirely.
**Group by generation, or the total silently answers a question nobody asked.**

## ⚠️ `doc` is serving bge-large, not voyage-4

- **`bin/build_generation.sh`** hardcoded `fastembed:BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5` and was dated
  2026-08-17. Running it against this corpus would have built a wrong-model generation in silence.
  It now refuses with an explanation; override is `BUILD_GENERATION_I_KNOW_IT_IS_STALE=1`, and the
  original is `bin/build_generation.sh.pre-voyage.bak`.
- **`bin/index_memory.sh`** line 156 counted `chunks` alone and printed "corpus: 9687 chunks" while
  the live corpus held 46,190. It now prints `RECALL_ENV`, both tables and the active generation.
  Original at `bin/index_memory.sh.pre-generations.bak`.

**PR [#221](https://github.com/GiulioDER/RE-call/pull/221) MERGED** as `6e1a736`, 2026-08-06.
Detail lives in `docs/ENTERPRISE_PROGRAM_STATUS.md` on master; this is the pointer plus what is not
in there.

## The result

**No context mode alters the raw chunk content or the raw content hashes it stores.** Three
independent comparisons against `bge-small-symmetric-v1`, over the corpus and glob the promotion
campaign used: **746 sources, 21,924 chunks per generation, 0 missing, 0 extra, 0 hash mismatches**,
equal chunk counts, on all three. Archived at
`/var/lib/recall-benchmarks/2026-08-06-context-mode-generation-parity/`, 8 of 8 files verify.

Measured 2026-08-22 on VPS2's `recall_repos`:

```sql
SELECT left(source,3), count(*) FROM chunks WHERE tenant_id='memory' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
--  C:\   9449
--  /ho      5
```

**Why this matters the moment embedding moves to VPS2** ([[embedding-runs-on-vps2-one-at-a-time]]).
`source` is the row key `replace_sources` DELETEs by and the key `source_content_hashes()` compares
against, so a corpus embedded under one path and re-indexed under another does not update: it
writes a second copy of every chunk, every file looks unseen and is re-embedded, and every search
that finds one of those memos returns it twice. This is not a prediction. The mirror image of it
was measured the same day in the other direction: **452 duplicate rows in `recall` and 615 in

`77c918cd93f9200b36e505ae874d49a1949f04a8a85ce5b8b72a8c135b472db7` and is unchanged across all
four of its generations, so a rebuild would reuse every unmoved file rather than re-embed.

Row counts for `memory`: **46,190 in `recall_chunks_v1`** and **9,687 in `chunks`** (dormant, the
pre-production corpus). Both exist. Counting only the second is the trap below.

🔁 **Corrected 2026-08-25: 46,190 is NOT the live corpus, it is the table total across all six
generations, and the live one is 9,608.** `recall_chunks_v1` is keyed by `generation_id` and
retains retired and ready generations, by design, so a bare `count(*)` over the table is 4.8x the
corpus any query can actually reach:

| state | corpus_version | chunks |
|---|---|---:|
| retired | memory-2026-08-17 | 8,671 |
| retired | memory-2026-08-20 | 9,053 |
| ready | memory-2026-08-22-voyage | 9,411 |
| retired | memory-2026-08-22-voyage-r2 | 9,444 |
| failed | memory-2026-08-22-voyage-r2 | 3 |
| **active** | **memory-20260824-voyage-r3** | **9,608** |

🔑 Note the shape of this one: the fix for "the check counted the wrong table" (`chunks`, 9,687)
was to count the right table — and 9,687 and 9,608 are within 1% of each other, so the corrected
check produced a number that *looked* like confirmation while being a different quantity entirely.
**Group by generation, or the total silently answers a question nobody asked.**

## ⚠️ `doc` is serving bge-large, not voyage-4

- **`bin/build_generation.sh`** hardcoded `fastembed:BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5` and was dated
  2026-08-17. Running it against this corpus would have built a wrong-model generation in silence.
  It now refuses with an explanation; override is `BUILD_GENERATION_I_KNOW_IT_IS_STALE=1`, and the
  original is `bin/build_generation.sh.pre-voyage.bak`.
- **`bin/index_memory.sh`** line 156 counted `chunks` alone and printed "corpus: 9687 chunks" while
  the live corpus held 46,190. It now prints `RECALL_ENV`, both tables and the active generation.
  Original at `bin/index_memory.sh.pre-generations.bak`.

**PR [#221](https://github.com/GiulioDER/RE-call/pull/221) MERGED** as `6e1a736`, 2026-08-06.
Detail lives in `docs/ENTERPRISE_PROGRAM_STATUS.md` on master; this is the pointer plus what is not
in there.

## The result

**No context mode alters the raw chunk content or the raw content hashes it stores.** Three
independent comparisons against `bge-small-symmetric-v1`, over the corpus and glob the promotion
campaign used: **746 sources, 21,924 chunks per generation, 0 missing, 0 extra, 0 hash mismatches**,
equal chunk counts, on all three. Archived at
`/var/lib/recall-benchmarks/2026-08-06-context-mode-generation-parity/`, 8 of 8 files verify.

Measured 2026-08-22 on VPS2's `recall_repos`:

```sql
SELECT left(source,3), count(*) FROM chunks WHERE tenant_id='memory' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
--  C:\   9449
--  /ho      5
```

**Why this matters the moment embedding moves to VPS2** ([[embedding-runs-on-vps2-one-at-a-time]]).
`source` is the row key `replace_sources` DELETEs by and the key `source_content_hashes()` compares
against, so a corpus embedded under one path and re-indexed under another does not update: it
writes a second copy of every chunk, every file looks unseen and is re-embedded, and every search
that finds one of those memos returns it twice. This is not a prediction. The mirror image of it
was measured the same day in the other direction: **452 duplicate rows in `recall` and 615 in

runs sync, rebuild, calibrate, promote and VERIFIES the corpus matches the active generation; scheduled task `recall-memory-refresh` fires it hourly, debounced to 6h on success, so an unclosed session no longer strands the corpus.
- [Generation gc is step 6 of the memory pipeline](generation-gc-is-step-6-of-the-memory-pipeline.md) — `recall generation gc` existed with zero callers while ~15 generations of chunk rows accumulated; since 2026-08-27 it runs after every promote (retention-days 2, retain-previous 2, best-effort, under embed.lock); READY generations need `abandon` first, and `--check` now prints the awaiting-gc count.
- [A script edited while running dies with a garbled syntax error](a-script-edited-while-running-dies-with-a-garbled-syntax-error.md) — bash reads scripts lazily,

memory pipeline. The right fix is a flock on the
  docs side; the memory side can only narrow the window.
- **Nothing retires old generations**: `recall_chunks_v1` held 143,985 rows across ~14
  generations for a 1,286-file corpus. Putting the rebuild on a schedule turns that into
  unbounded growth. Tracked separately.

Related: [[embedding-runs-on-vps2-one-at-a-time]], [[vps2-memory-refresh-is-the-generation-chain]],
[[stop-proposing-to-rebuild-the-corpus]].

Measured 2026-08-25 on VPS2 with the correct embedder: `recall.cli search` prints
`generation=legacy` and reads the legacy **`chunks`** table (9,687 rows for `memory`, last indexed
2026-08-24), while the server reads **`recall_chunks_v1`** at the certified active generation
(9,608 rows). **Two corpora, 0.8% apart in size, both plausible, both answering.** The CLI's
results are ungated: no generation binding, no certified threshold, no `trust_state` at all.

🔑 So "I tested it with the CLI" is not a test of what a session gets, and the sizes are close
enough that no sanity check on the result count will catch it. Use the CLI to look things up; use
the SERVER, or `scripts/session-corpus.sh status`, to make any claim about what is served.

seconds and dragged the mean 33 seconds negative.

**Why it is a real hazard and not pedantry.** These values are serialised straight to JSON and the
JSON backs preregistered benchmark results. If `elapsed_ms` had been an `int`, then `float()`
emitted `1.0` and `cast` emits `1`. Nothing raises, no test necessarily notices, and a committed
results artifact quietly changes shape. The same applies to `int(x)` over a string, `str(x)` over
bytes, and `bool(x)` over a container: each was doing work that `cast` does not do.

**What I actually did, and the general form of it.** Traced every value back to its assignment
before touching it:

```
elapsed_ms, baseline_ms, treatment_ms   (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000.0   -> already float
forbidden_selected                      len(case.forbidden_ids & ids)              -> already int
```

Still open, verdicts and evidence in the status file: AUD-2 reranker absent from the manifest ·
AUD-3 the resume guard compares row COUNTS not identities, so reusing `--table-prefix` across a
changed corpus passes on a mixed index · AUD-4 per-arm `elapsed_s` includes writing and scoring, so
it is not retrieval time (the `latency_ms` percentiles are unaffected) · AUD-5 the harness can
fetch model weights at runtime, which the program's own out-of-scope list forbids · AUD-6 no module
docstring so `--help` renders empty · AUD-7 `p95` floors to the 94.87th percentile at n=507 ·
AUD-8 a bounded connection leak on the setup exception path.

Found 2026-08-21 by chasing a p-value that looked wrong: wall time reported **mean -33,035 ms with
p=0.9473**. That is not a combination a well-behaved sample produces, and the test was right.

| metric | mean | median |
|---|---|---|
| input_tokens | -2,293 | **+14,904** |
| wall_time_ms | -33,035 | **+1,703** |
| model_turns | -1 | **0** |

The on arm was **slower in 29 of 48 pairs**. A handful of baseline sessions went exploring for 400
seconds and dragged the mean 33 seconds negative.

**Why it is a real hazard and not pedantry.** These values are serialised straight to JSON and the
JSON backs preregistered benchmark results. If `elapsed_ms` had been an `int`, then `float()`
emitted `1.0` and `cast` emits `1`. Nothing raises, no test necessarily notices, and a committed
results artifact quietly changes shape. The same applies to `int(x)` over a string, `str(x)` over
bytes, and `bool(x)` over a container: each was doing work that `cast` does not do.

**What I actually did, and the general form of it.** Traced every value back to its assignment
before touching it:

```
elapsed_ms, baseline_ms, treatment_ms   (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000.0   -> already float
forbidden_selected                      len(case.forbidden_ids & ids)              -> already int
```

commit, because the three commits it describes were rebased onto master an hour later and every
hash written here first is already wrong.

| Run | pytest clock | wall |
|---|---|---|
| serial | 49:58 | 52:27 |
| `-n 4` | 14:05 | 14:20 |
| `-n 6` | 16:45 and 21:08 | worker killed in BOTH |

**`typing.cast` returns its argument untouched. `float()` and `int()` do not. Swapping one for the
other to satisfy mypy is only safe when the value is ALREADY the target type, and that has to be
checked, not assumed.**

2026-08-19 in recall, clearing 10 mypy errors so PR #425 could go green. Benchmark probes returned
`dict[str, object]`, so `float(row["elapsed_ms"])` failed with *Argument 1 to "float" has

row.original_prompt: Write `scripts/bounded.py` which takes a command and its arguments, runs it, and gives up after 3 seconds. On giving up it must print TIMEOUT and exit 124; otherwise it passes through the command's own exit code. It guards a pre-commit hook, so returning promptly is the whole point of it. items.text:
`subprocess.run(..., timeout=3)` does **not** bound wall-clock time. It kills the direct child only.
Any grandchild that inherited the stdout pipe keeps `communicate()` blocked, so the read never
finishes.

Measured 2026-08-16: `run([bash, script], timeout=3)` where the script body was `sleep 45` took
**45.2 seconds**. `bash` was killed on schedule; `sleep` held the pipe. A script that merely
backgrounds `sleep 30 &` and exits immediately blocks for the full 30s the same way.

Two consequences worth separating:

- [bash from Python reaches WSL, not Git Bash](bash-from-python-reaches-wsl.md) — CreateProcess searches System32 before PATH, so `subprocess(["bash",...])` dies with execvpe(/bin/bash) while `shutil.which` reports Git Bash. Resolve an absolute path.

hits.text:
`subprocess.run(..., timeout=3)` does **not** bound wall-clock time. It kills the direct child only.
Any grandchild that inherited the stdout pipe keeps `communicate()` blocked, so the read never
finishes.

Measured 2026-08-16: `run([bash, script], timeout=3)` where the script body was `sleep 45` took
**45.2 seconds**. `bash` was killed on schedule; `sleep` held the pipe. A script that merely
backgrounds `sleep 30 &` and exits immediately blocks for the full 30s the same way.

Two consequences worth separating:

1. **The timeout is enforced against the wrong process.** Kill the **tree**: `taskkill /T /F /PID`
   on Windows, `killpg` elsewhere, then drain with a short second timeout.
2. **A slow command gets misreported as a broken one.** With a launch-failure sentinel, a command
   that eventually returns after the timeout comes back as "never ran", which is a different fact
   and sends the caller down a different path.

**Per-command timeouts do not compose.** A dozen commands at 20s each is four minutes in front of a
user. Anything on a latency-sensitive path (a SessionStart hook, a pre-commit guard) needs a single
whole-run budget that later steps check before spawning anything, plus `stdin=DEVNULL` so a child
that prompts for a credential fails instead of hanging.

- **A watch command exits on transport failure exactly as it exits on success.** The check states in
  the buffer were the last ones it managed to fetch, so the output *looked* like a status report and
  was actually a snapshot from before the error.
- **The wrapper hid the exit status.** The command was
  `gh pr checks --watch > log 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; tail -15 log`, and the harness reported the exit
  code of the LAST command in the chain, `tail`, which is always 0. Same shape as the pipe trap in
  [[master-lives-in-a-separate-worktree]]: a command whose status you care about must not be
  followed by one whose status you do not.

🔑 **Read the SKIP COUNT, not only the pass count.** 32 is healthy here; `CLAUDE.md` says roughly 22
and warns that several hundred means the DB tests never ran and the reason is printed in the skip
text.

retrieval.query: bounded timeout subprocess command timeout exit code

hits.text:
`subprocess.run(..., timeout=3)` does **not** bound wall-clock time. It kills the direct child only.
Any grandchild that inherited the stdout pipe keeps `communicate()` blocked, so the read never
finishes.

Measured 2026-08-16: `run([bash, script], timeout=3)` where the script body was `sleep 45` took
**45.2 seconds**. `bash` was killed on schedule; `sleep` held the pipe. A script that merely
backgrounds `sleep 30 &` and exits immediately blocks for the full 30s the same way.

Two consequences worth separating:

- [bash from Python reaches WSL, not Git Bash](bash-from-python-reaches-wsl.md) — CreateProcess searches System32 before PATH, so `subprocess(["bash",...])` dies with execvpe(/bin/bash) while `shutil.which` reports Git Bash. Resolve an absolute path.
- [noclobber IS atomic here; the race was elsewhere](noclobber-is-not-atomic-on-msys.md) — 🔁 corrected 2026-08-22: re-measured with 12 barrier-released racers, `set -C` admits exactly one winner. The four winners came from a check-then-act race OUTSIDE the lock. A concurrency claim measured without a barrier has not been measured.
- [subprocess timeout does not bound wall clock](subprocess-timeout-does-not-bound-wall-clock.md) — a 3s timeout took 45.2s because killing bash left `sleep` holding the pipe. Kill the tree, and give

- **A watch command exits on transport failure exactly as it exits on success.** The check states in
  the buffer were the last ones it managed to fetch, so the output *looked* like a status report and
  was actually a snapshot from before the error.
- **The wrapper hid the exit status.** The command was
  `gh pr checks --watch > log 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; tail -15 log`, and the harness reported the exit
  code of the LAST command in the chain, `tail`, which is always 0. Same shape as the pipe trap in
  [[master-lives-in-a-separate-worktree]]: a command whose status you care about must not be
  followed by one whose status you do not.

🔑 **Read the SKIP COUNT, not only the pass count.** 32 is healthy here; `CLAUDE.md` says roughly 22
and warns that several hundred means the DB tests never ran and the reason is printed in the skip
text.

## Re-measure

```bash
eval "$(scripts/session-db.sh up)" && export RECALL_TEST_DSN
python -m pytest tests/ -q --timeout=300 > /tmp/fullsuite.log 2>&1; echo "EXIT: $?"
tail -3 /tmp/fullsuite.log
scripts/session-db.sh down
```

⚠️ **Redirect, never pipe**, if you intend to read the exit code: a pipeline reports the LAST
command's status. And allow at least 40 minutes.

⛔ **Not yet corrected in the repository.** `CLAUDE.md:140` still says 12 minutes; fixing it is a
one line pull request nobody has opened. Until then this memo is the accurate number.

**Measured 2026-08-18** on this Windows workstation, with a session container:

```
5694 passed, 32 skipped in 1857.08s (0:30:57)
```

`CLAUDE.md:140` states "The full suite takes about **12 minutes** with a database and about 5
without." That is **stale by a factor of two and a half**, and it is a claim in a file loaded into
every session, so it is believed by default.

## Why it matters beyond the number

A 15 or 20 minute timeout looks generous against the documented figure and **kills the run at
roughly two thirds**. That is exactly what happened here on the first attempt, and the killed run
then reported success because its exit code came from a `| tail` rather than from pytest. Two
independent defects lined up to turn "the suite did not finish" into "the suite passed".

1. **The timeout is enforced against the wrong process.** Kill the **tree**: `taskkill /T /F /PID`
   on Windows, `killpg` elsewhere, then drain with a short second timeout.
2. **A slow command gets misreported as a broken one.** With a launch-failure sentinel, a command
   that eventually returns after the timeout comes back as "never ran", which is a different fact
   and sends the caller down a different path.

user. Anything on a latency-sensitive path (a SessionStart hook, a pre-commit guard) needs a single
whole-run budget that later steps check before spawning anything, plus `stdin=DEVNULL` so a child
that prompts for a credential fails instead of hanging.

**1. "Flat CPU means it is stalled." No.** The parent burns **1.8s of its own CPU for 25s of real
work (7.4%)**, because the work is charged to 178 `git.exe` children. `Get-Process python | Select
CPU` reports only the parent, so a healthy subprocess-bound run looks identical to a hang. I read
3.16s of parent CPU over 15 minutes as proof of a stall and **killed a suite that was fine** at 28%.
Use wall-clock progress, or watch for child processes, never parent CPU.

**2. "git index.lock contention with my own commit/push." No.** The stack was inside
`Thread.start()`, which is subprocess's Windows reader-thread setup and runs **before git is ever
executed**. git cannot have been the blocker. I asserted this to the user as the confirmed cause.

**Sorting a random sample and then stopping early is not sampling. It is taking the head.**

The shape, which looks harmless in review:

```python
for i in sorted(rng.sample(range(len(items)), pool_size)):
    if len(kept) == target:      # or: if too_big: break
        break
    kept.append(i)
```

The sort is usually added for a good reason (stable output order, corpus order in a prompt). The
early stop is usually added for a good reason (a target count, a size budget). **Together they mean
only the lowest-indexed part of the sample is ever considered**, and the more you oversample the
worse it gets, because the tail moves further out of reach.

2. Backfill scoring runs head on ALL chunks (including those in train set)

oversized item does not end the selection, and sort only the KEPT subset afterwards if presentation

## Schema (`code_chunks`)
- `id BIGSERIAL`, `path TEXT`, `language TEXT` (`python|markdown|sql`),
  `chunk_idx INT`, `start_line INT`, `end_line INT`, `content TEXT`,
  `content_tsv tsvector` (BM25), `embedding vector(1024)`, `sha256 TEXT`,
  `mtime TIMESTAMPTZ`, `created_at TIMESTAMPTZ`.
- Unique key: `(path, sha256)` — content-addressed, idempotent reindex.
- HNSW index `code_chunks_embedding_hnsw` on `embedding` (cosine).

RE-call's evidence prompt wrapped a `json.dumps` payload in `<evidence_data>` … `</evidence_data>`
and handed it to a generator. `json.dumps` escapes `"`, `\` and control characters. It does **not**
escape `<` or `>`, and the delimiter is built from exactly those two characters.

A memory whose text, file name or chunk id contained `</evidence_data>` **closed the region early**,
and everything after it reached the model as free prose in its own instruction channel. Reproduced
by rendering one hit: the message contained two closing tags. `ensure_ascii=True` does not help —
it escapes non-ASCII, and `<` is ASCII.

**Delimiting without escaping the delimiter is not delimiting.**

Nothing records which extractor ran: chunk metadata carries `source_format`, `extraction` and
`media_type` but no library versions, and `STRUCTURED_DOCUMENT_VERSION` versions recall's own block
shape only. **So no existing non-markdown corpus can be attested**, and re extraction alone cannot
distinguish "the extractor changed" from "the file is wrong". Same shape as
[[embedding-profile-id-lies-for-unregistered-models]]: fixing a writer does not repair rows already
written.

Related: [[chunker-is-not-in-the-index-fingerprint]] for the markdown half, which *is* attestable.

🔑 **A corpus can hold chunks from SEVERAL chunker eras at once, and that is the NORMAL result of
any chunker change, not an exotic case.** It follows directly from the omission above: the run after
the change skips every unchanged file, so those keep their old chunking while newly changed files
get the new one. Anything that must assert one `ChunkerIdentity` for a whole corpus (a generation's
`PipelineIdentity` carries exactly one) therefore cannot assume homogeneity. Check per source.

    --from-jsonl test_chunks.jsonl --out /tmp/replay.jsonl

### Phase B ready for vast.ai (commits 9517f1e)
- **corpus_extractor.py** ran on VPS2: 103 776 dedupped chunks, 256.9M chars in 13s. Earnings_transcripts skipped (schema mismatch — non-blocker).
- **tokenizer_audit.py** ran on VPS2: 57.5M tokens, mean 554 tok/chunk, p99=1279 tok, max 2997 tok. Distribuzione 10-Q 30.7M / 10-K 24.1M / 8-K 2.7M.
- **Wall-time stim. Phase B** 1 epoca QLoRA r=8 max_seq=4096:
  - 1× 5090 ≈ 32h
  - **4× 5090 ≈ 9.6h** (sweet spot)
  - 8× 5090 ≈ 6h (NCCL overhead diminishing returns)
- **Costo Phase B su vast.ai**: ~$30–40 per 4×5090 a $3-4/h × 10h.

4. **Different prediction horizon** — h=20d or h=60d may have higher signal-to-noise than h=5d.
5. **Different consumption format** — Anthropic-style "contextual retrieval" with chunk-level metadata prepended pre-embedding.

**How to apply:** when a session asks "where does X live / who calls Y / what
pattern handles Z", run `--code-search` *before* grep. Grep still wins for
exact-string lookups (typos, error messages, identifiers you already know).

## Schema (`code_chunks`)
- `id BIGSERIAL`, `path TEXT`, `language TEXT` (`python|markdown|sql`),
  `chunk_idx INT`, `start_line INT`, `end_line INT`, `content TEXT`,
  `content_tsv tsvector` (BM25), `embedding vector(1024)`, `sha256 TEXT`,
  `mtime TIMESTAMPTZ`, `created_at TIMESTAMPTZ`.
- Unique key: `(path, sha256)` — content-addressed, idempotent reindex.
- HNSW index `code_chunks_embedding_hnsw` on `embedding` (cosine).

**First run (bug)**: Parse 51% (151/294), match 77.5% on parsable. Output for ~143 chunks was filing-text continuation instead of JSON.

**Root cause**: user content ≈4000 tokens, `max_length=2048` truncated mid-prompt; chat-template assistant marker survived but model lost context (system prompt + part of filing). truncation_side="left" attempt also failed — model still emitted continuation.

**Fix**: bump `max_length=8192` (Qwen2.5 supports 32K, vast.ai 5090 has VRAM). No truncation actually happens on the test set (avg 5K tokens), prompt arrives intact.

Found on 2026-08-15 fixing `recall index`, which chose the chunker from the GLOB SUFFIX
(`chunk_code if args.glob.endswith(".py") else chunk_text`) rather than per file, so
`--glob '**/*'` chunked every `.py` as prose and said nothing. Fixed by `chunker_for_path`, with
the non-repair noted in its docstring so the next person does not assume a re-index is enough.

⚠️ `chunk_code` is **Python-specific**: it starts a block at a column-0 `def`/`class`/`@`/`async
def`. Given Rust, SQL or shell it matches nothing, returns one block, and is strictly worse than
`chunk_text`, which at least splits on blank lines. Do not widen `PYTHON_SUFFIXES` without a
chunker that parses the language being added.

- VPS2 dense plus lexical indexing effectively completed with `519,245` chunks and `511,958` distinct doc ids in `ber_voy_lex_12k_full`. The official text ZIP had `511,962` text files, so the four-file gap is likely duplicate source id collapse, not a visible ingestion crash.
- The first answer phase crashed before producing rows because Voyage `rerank-2.5` rejected a batch with `602,735` tokens, above its `600,000` token batch cap.
- Commit `6b88292` caps rerank candidate document text with `--rerank-document-chars`, default `4000`.

### 2026-08-12 SPLADE GPU preparation update

**Sorting a random sample and then stopping early is not sampling. It is taking the head.**

The shape, which looks harmless in review:

```python
for i in sorted(rng.sample(range(len(items)), pool_size)):
    if len(kept) == target:      # or: if too_big: break
        break
    kept.append(i)
```

The sort is usually added for a good reason (stable output order, corpus order in a prompt). The
early stop is usually added for a good reason (a target count, a size budget). **Together they mean
only the lowest-indexed part of the sample is ever considered**, and the more you oversample the
worse it gets, because the tail moves further out of reach.

Measured twice on recall's own `docs/` (1815 chunks over 51 files):

- **Before writing that a source is unreproducible, read its method section.** That claim requires
  the body; it cannot be made from an abstract.
- **Attribute per source.** When a fact arrives from a comment, cite the comment. Two sources
  merging into one attribution is how a weak claim inherits a strong one's authority.
- arXiv PDFs are readable here: `WebFetch` on `/pdf/<id>` returns binary but **saves the file
  locally** and prints the path, and `pypdf` is installed, so
  `PdfReader(path)` plus `extract_text()` gives the full text in one step.
- Correct in place with a 🔁 marker naming the direction of the error, rather than swapping the text
  silently. Which way I was wrong is the reusable part.

⛔ **Do not hand-write rows into `recall_chunks_v1` to trigger reuse.** The schema gap is only
five columns (`generation_id, source_uri, object_version_id, source_sha256, chunk_ordinal`) and
the embeddings already exist, so it is tempting and cheap. It also fabricates the provenance a
generation exists to ESTABLISH, the same false-immutability trap `lineage.py` refuses for
`file://` objects.

**The build path that works** (needs `RECALL_LOCAL_ALLOWLIST` set to the corpus root):

```bash
recall --tenant T manifest create --corpus-version V --objects objs.json --output m.json
recall --tenant T generation build m.json --manifest-sha256 S --manifest-size N \
  --embedder-provider fastembed --embedder-revision R --embedder-artifact-digest D --project P
```

### 2026-08-12 SPLADE GPU preparation update

**Sorting a random sample and then stopping early is not sampling. It is taking the head.**

The shape, which looks harmless in review:

```python
for i in sorted(rng.sample(range(len(items)), pool_size)):
    if len(kept) == target:      # or: if too_big: break
        break
    kept.append(i)
```

The sort is usually added for a good reason (stable output order, corpus order in a prompt). The
early stop is usually added for a good reason (a target count, a size budget). **Together they mean
only the lowest-indexed part of the sample is ever considered**, and the more you oversample the
worse it gets, because the tail moves further out of reach.

Measured twice on recall's own `docs/` (1815 chunks over 51 files):

| site | sorted + early stop | sampled + continue |
|---|---|---|
| `queryset.generate_offline` chunk sampling | **3 of 51 files** | 21 of 51 |
| `llm.generate_llm` prompt budget trim | **3 of 51 files** | 21 of 51 |

Identical numbers, identical cause, two separate commits days apart. The second one was written
*after* fixing the first and after documenting the lesson in a comment three files away.

**The fix is always the same:** iterate in sampled order, use `continue` rather than `break` so one
oversized item does not end the selection, and sort only the KEPT subset afterwards if presentation
order matters.

Found on 2026-08-15 fixing `recall index`, which chose the chunker from the GLOB SUFFIX
(`chunk_code if args.glob.endswith(".py") else chunk_text`) rather than per file, so
`--glob '**/*'` chunked every `.py` as prose and said nothing. Fixed by `chunker_for_path`, with
the non-repair noted in its docstring so the next person does not assume a re-index is enough.

⚠️ `chunk_code` is **Python-specific**: it starts a block at a column-0 `def`/`class`/`@`/`async
def`. Given Rust, SQL or shell it matches nothing, returns one block, and is strictly worse than
`chunk_text`, which at least splits on blank lines. Do not widen `PYTHON_SUFFIXES` without a
chunker that parses the language being added.

### 2026-08-12 SPLADE GPU preparation update

🔑 **A corpus can hold chunks from SEVERAL chunker eras at once, and that is the NORMAL result of
any chunker change, not an exotic case.** It follows directly from the omission above: the run after
the change skips every unchanged file, so those keep their old chunking while newly changed files
get the new one. Anything that must assert one `ChunkerIdentity` for a whole corpus (a generation's
`PipelineIdentity` carries exactly one) therefore cannot assume homogeneity. Check per source.

**Scelta 3a**: migrazione architetturale completa su Postgres + pgvector, single store.

Schema unico `rag_chunks`:
```sql
CREATE TABLE rag_chunks (
  chunk_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  ticker, filing_type, accession, section,
  chunk_index INT, filing_date DATE,
  text TEXT, text_hash CHAR(16) UNIQUE,
  token_count INT, is_table SMALLINT, table_title TEXT,
  embedding vector(1024),

-- GIN(fts), ivfflat(embedding, lists=200), (ticker,filing_date), (accession)

**Sorting a random sample and then stopping early is not sampling. It is taking the head.**

The shape, which looks harmless in review:

```python
for i in sorted(rng.sample(range(len(items)), pool_size)):
    if len(kept) == target:      # or: if too_big: break
        break
    kept.append(i)
```

The sort is usually added for a good reason (stable output order, corpus order in a prompt). The
early stop is usually added for a good reason (a target count, a size budget). **Together they mean
only the lowest-indexed part of the sample is ever considered**, and the more you oversample the
worse it gets, because the tail moves further out of reach.

Measured twice on recall's own `docs/` (1815 chunks over 51 files):

**First run (bug)**: Parse 51% (151/294), match 77.5% on parsable. Output for ~143 chunks was filing-text continuation instead of JSON.

**Root cause**: user content ≈4000 tokens, `max_length=2048` truncated mid-prompt; chat-template assistant marker survived but model lost context (system prompt + part of filing). truncation_side="left" attempt also failed — model still emitted continuation.

**Fix**: bump `max_length=8192` (Qwen2.5 supports 32K, vast.ai 5090 has VRAM). No truncation actually happens on the test set (avg 5K tokens), prompt arrives intact.

Identical numbers, identical cause, two separate commits days apart. The second one was written
*after* fixing the first and after documenting the lesson in a comment three files away.

**The fix is always the same:** iterate in sampled order, use `continue` rather than `break` so one
oversized item does not end the selection, and sort only the KEPT subset afterwards if presentation
order matters.

- **Data that must be disjoint from the corpus does not live in a globbed file type.** JSON, TOML,
  anything the code and docs globs miss.
- ⛔ **Do not quote the data in a comment either.** I re-poisoned the pool TWICE while fixing it, by
  naming example subjects in comments explaining the bug. The first cost three subjects and was
  caught only because a measured count moved the wrong way; a threshold guard stayed green because
  55 still cleared 40. Refer to the file; never quote it.
- **Guard on CAPACITY plus RARITY, not on zero overlap.** Demanding no subject word appear is
  unachievable (`tuning`, `timing`, `methods` are in any codebase) and counting
  subjects-disqualified-per-file fails on large modules for the same reason. The pool now declares a

marker survived for `bad.md` and was stripped for `sub/bad.md`. Every test used a root-level file,
so the suite stayed green while nested corpora were broken. I fixed it, and the very next guard

both; my tests could not have.

the input. A fixture that only ever builds files at the root never varies the one dimension the
code is sensitive to, so the tests agree with the bug.

each time: what does this new rule do to inputs that are legal but unusual, and does it survive the
normalisers downstream of it? Two of the four would have been caught by

I put a marker on a corpus-relative path; `supersedes_key` keeps only the last segment, so the
marker survived for `bad.md` and was stripped for `sub/bad.md`. Every test used a root-level file,
so the suite stayed green while nested corpora were broken. I fixed it, and the very next guard

both; my tests could not have.

**Why:** a normaliser that reduces structure (last segment, basename, stem) makes position part of
the input. A fixture that only ever builds files at the root never varies the one dimension the
code is sensitive to, so the tests agree with the bug.

each time: what does this new rule do to inputs that are legal but unusual, and does it survive the
normalisers downstream of it? Two of the four would have been caught by

into a failure whose message names uploads, indexing or whatever the fixture was for, in a test
about something else entirely.

Measured 2026-08-18 in recall while confining `RECALL_INDEX_ROOT` so the suite stopped writing
`uploads/acme/<job_id>/memo.md` into the checkout. The autouse fixture pointed the variable at
`tmp_path / "recall-index-root"` and created it. Full suite: **2 failed, 5455 passed**:
`tests/test_fix.py::test_apply_proposal_preserves_the_memo_when_the_write_fails` (asserts no temp
litter survives a failed write) and
`tests/test_bench_systems.py::test_conversation_to_messages_mirrors_recall_turn_walk` (reads every
entry in `tmp_path` as text, so a directory raises `PermissionError` on `read_text`). Neither test
touches uploads. Cost: one full 25 minute suite run.

Measured 2026-08-18 in recall. A report said `python -m pytest tests/` leaves an untracked
`uploads/acme/` in the repository root, observed in `.claude/worktrees/pr334-review`, and asked for
the relative write to be pointed at a fixture. Every fact in it was true **of that worktree**. The
fix had landed the same day in `295379fd` (#374): an autouse fixture confining `RECALL_INDEX_ROOT`
to a session-scoped temp dir, plus a regression guard at `tests/test_desktop.py:114`. `pr334-review`
was 19 behind master, its `conftest.py` had zero occurrences of `_confine_index_root`, and the
symptom was reproducing exactly as described. Two commands settled it; the hunt would have taken an
hour and produced a second, conflicting fix.

An autouse fixture must not create anything inside `tmp_path`. `tmp_path` belongs to the test, and
tests assert on **all** of it: `list(tmp_path.iterdir()) == [memo]`, or a dict comprehension over
`sorted(tmp_path.iterdir())` that then reads each entry as a file. One extra directory turns both
into a failure whose message names uploads, indexing or whatever the fixture was for, in a test
about something else entirely.

runs green ("indexed
   250 chunks from 26 files") and writes the legacy `chunks` table. The CLI finds the memo; the
   server's next search still ABSTAINS on it.
2. MCP `recall_index` refuses: "local filesystem indexing is development-only".
3. MCP `recall_ingest` refuses for hosted embedders: "production generation builds require an
   immutable embedder revision or artifact digest".
4. `bash index_memory_vps2.sh` dies at its FIRST store alphabetically, so nothing at all is
   indexed, and `sync_memstores.sh` has already reported success by then. Worse, its `--check`
   prints `guards held` while the real run refuses: **`--check` is not evidence that indexing
   will work.**


**How to apply:** the full chain is written into `~/.claude/commands/session-close.md` step 5

Also corrects [[vps2-serves-three-tenants-doc-memory-code]], written by me earlier the same day,
which recorded the user's shorthand as if it were the tenant ids. `doc` and `code` are
`re-call-docs` and `re-call-code-gen`.

## ⛔ The open problem: nothing here can index a new memo

`index_memory_vps2.sh` calls `recall index`, which writes the legacy `chunks` table and is refused
under production by `_cmd_index` in `recall/cli_commands/index_search.py:202`:

```
local filesystem indexing is development-only; build from an immutable S3 manifest in production
```

Measured 2026-08-18 in recall. A report said `python -m pytest tests/` leaves an untracked
`uploads/acme/` in the repository root, observed in `.claude/worktrees/pr334-review`, and asked for
the relative write to be pointed at a fixture. Every fact in it was true **of that worktree**. The
fix had landed the same day in `295379fd` (#374): an autouse fixture confining `RECALL_INDEX_ROOT`
to a session-scoped temp dir, plus a regression guard at `tests/test_desktop.py:114`. `pr334-review`
was 19 behind master, its `conftest.py` had zero occurrences of `_confine_index_root`, and the
symptom was reproducing exactly as described. Two commands settled it; the hunt would have taken an
hour and produced a second, conflicting fix.

Measured 2026-08-18 in recall while confining `RECALL_INDEX_ROOT` so the suite stopped writing
`uploads/acme/<job_id>/memo.md` into the checkout. The autouse fixture pointed the variable at
`tmp_path / "recall-index-root"` and created it. Full suite: **2 failed, 5455 passed**:
`tests/test_fix.py::test_apply_proposal_preserves_the_memo_when_the_write_fails` (asserts no temp
litter survives a failed write) and
`tests/test_bench_systems.py::test_conversation_to_messages_mirrors_recall_turn_walk` (reads every
entry in `tmp_path` as text, so a directory raises `PermissionError` on `read_text`). Neither test
touches uploads. Cost: one full 25 minute suite run.

An autouse fixture must not create anything inside `tmp_path`. `tmp_path` belongs to the test, and
tests assert on **all** of it: `list(tmp_path.iterdir()) == [memo]`, or a dict comprehension over
`sorted(tmp_path.iterdir())` that then reads each entry as a file. One extra directory turns both
into a failure whose message names uploads, indexing or whatever the fixture was for, in a test
about something else entirely.

The fix is a session-scoped `tmp_path_factory.mktemp(...)` handed to the autouse fixture, so the
suite-wide default lives outside every test's scratch space. Session scope is safe when the writes
are uuid-keyed; a per-test directory under the factory root is the alternative if they are not.

**Why:** a suite-wide fixture is invisible at the failure site, so the debugging starts in the wrong
file. The two tests above read as flaky or as regressions in `apply_proposal` and the LOCOMO walk.

**Every existing test created the directory in its own fixture.** `root = tmp_path / "project";
root.mkdir()` is what a test writes without thinking, because a test needs somewhere to look. So
the entire suite was structurally incapable of noticing that production code never created it, and
being green meant nothing about this. It took a clean-room CI job pointed at
`$RUNNER_TEMP/install/project` — a path nothing had ever made — to find it.

**So: a suite whose fixtures pre-create the resource cannot test who creates the resource.** When
the bug is "nothing creates X", assert on an X that has deliberately never been created, and say
so in the test:

```python
assert not project_root.exists(), "the point of this test is that nothing has created it"
```

Measured 2026-08-18 in recall while confining `RECALL_INDEX_ROOT` so the suite stopped writing
`uploads/acme/<job_id>/memo.md` into the checkout. The autouse fixture pointed the variable at
`tmp_path / "recall-index-root"` and created it. Full suite: **2 failed, 5455 passed**:
`tests/test_fix.py::test_apply_proposal_preserves_the_memo_when_the_write_fails` (asserts no temp
litter survives a failed write) and
`tests/test_bench_systems.py::test_conversation_to_messages_mirrors_recall_turn_walk` (reads every
entry in `tmp_path` as text, so a directory raises `PermissionError` on `read_text`). Neither test
touches uploads. Cost: one full 25 minute suite run.

An autouse fixture must not create anything inside `tmp_path`. `tmp_path` belongs to the test, and
tests assert on **all** of it: `list(tmp_path.iterdir()) == [memo]`, or a dict comprehension over
`sorted(tmp_path.iterdir())` that then reads each entry as a file. One extra directory turns both
into a failure whose message names uploads, indexing or whatever the fixture was for, in a test
about something else entirely.

**Every existing test created the directory in its own fixture.** `root = tmp_path / "project";
root.mkdir()` is what a test writes without thinking, because a test needs somewhere to look. So
the entire suite was structurally incapable of noticing that production code never created it, and
being green meant nothing about this. It took a clean-room CI job pointed at
`$RUNNER_TEMP/install/project` — a path nothing had ever made — to find it.

**So: a suite whose fixtures pre-create the resource cannot test who creates the resource.** When
the bug is "nothing creates X", assert on an X that has deliberately never been created, and say
so in the test:

```python
assert not project_root.exists(), "the point of this test is that nothing has created it"
```

The fix is a session-scoped `tmp_path_factory.mktemp(...)` handed to the autouse fixture, so the
suite-wide default lives outside every test's scratch space. Session scope is safe when the writes
are uuid-keyed; a per-test directory under the factory root is the alternative if they are not.

**Why:** a suite-wide fixture is invisible at the failure site, so the debugging starts in the wrong
file. The two tests above read as flaky or as regressions in `apply_proposal` and the LOCOMO walk.
